preamble: The voiced palatal plosive [ɟ] becomes the voiced postalveolar fricative [ʒ] through spirantization. The clearest case is Arabic jīm. Proto-Semitic *g had become palatal /ɡʲ/ or /ɟ/ by the time of the Quran (Watson 2002). After the early conquests it gave [ʒ] in urban Levantine and most Northwest African dialects, while other dialects have [d͡ʒ], [ɡ] or kept [ɟ]. French jour (< diurnum) reaches [ʒ] by a different chain, [j] > Old French [d͡ʒ] > [ʒ], so it belongs under j_affricate_to_zh.

examples.note: جمل 'camel'; compare Standard Arabic /d͡ʒamal/ and Egyptian /ɡamal/.
جبل 'mountain'; the short vowel of the first syllable is also lost.

sources: Watson, J. C. E. (2002). The Phonology and Morphology of Arabic. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780199257591.001.0001
